extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophers, scientists, and anyone assessing inductive reasoning or argument quality
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying and critiquing faulty generalizations and inductive inferences (fallacies such as simple enumeration, false analogy, post hoc, and inappropriate reduction). Applicable to evaluating arguments, scientific inference, witness testimony, and social/political theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perception from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers (especially untrained ones) commonly intermingle hypotheses and inferences with the narrative of their sensory perceptions; a genuine specification of phenomena should be unsophisticated by fancy or preconceived opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require reports and testimony to separate raw sensory detail from interpretive claims. Trained observers can specify sensations plainly; lay witnesses often unconsciously describe theories rather than mere perceptions. Anti-pattern: accepting narrative evidence that embeds theoretical vocabulary as if it were direct observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extrapolating local order to the remote universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from the order of nature on Earth or in the solar system to remote parts of the universe are not warranted by experience and therefore must be regarded as groundless unless independent evidence supports them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume phenomena or laws observed locally hold universally without justification. Treat assertions about remote or radically different domains as speculative unless supported by specific inductive evidence from those domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert universal negatives from absence of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-existence of a phenomenon in observed experience proves at most that no adequate cause has yet manifested itself; absence of evidence is not evidence of impossibility except where mathematical/size/extension laws or the universal law of causality apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from concluding impossibility from lack of observed instances. Only allow impossibility claims when they rest on inviolable numeric/extension laws or proven causal impossibility. Anti-pattern: declaring something 'impossible' merely because it has not yet been seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid resolving radically different phenomena into one element (illegitimate reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorizing that reduces qualitatively different phenomena (different in kind, not merely degree) to a single element or mode (e.g., explaining sensation entirely as motion) is generally false unless it shows more than mere antecedent-condition relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between establishing that one phenomenon is a condition or cause of another (which may be legitimate) and claiming that the generic peculiarities of a phenomenon are eliminated by reducing it to another kind. Anti-patterns: treating sensations, consciousness, life, or qualitative properties as exhaustively explained by motion/mechanics without accounting for their distinct character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by mere enumeration—listing observed instances and concluding the universal (e.g., 'these A are B, therefore all A are B')—is a rudimentary and precarious method of reasoning unless accompanied by eliminations and exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require methods of rejection/exclusion and consideration of counter-instances before generalizing. Use elimination of alternative hypotheses, not just accumulation of supportive examples. Examples of the fallacy: hasty broad social maxims derived from limited, uneliminated samples. Scoring note: high-quality induction must show why contradictory instances are excluded and how the generalization is derived from underlying causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical (observational) laws from causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations express customary succession of effects within observed limits and are provisional; they are not equivalent to laws of causation, which explain why effects occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a purported law is merely an observed regularity (useful within adjacent cases) or a causal law deduced from identified causes. Prefer causal explanations for robust prediction; treat empirical laws as limited and contingent. Anti-pattern: treating empirical summaries as ultimate truths without seeking causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring causation from mere conjunction (post hoc/cum hoc fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that A causes B because A preceded B or co-occurred with B (post hoc, ergo propter hoc; cum hoc, ergo propter hoc) is invalid without elimination of alternative antecedents and independent causal reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand elimination of confounders, independent evidence of mechanism, or corroborating experiments before accepting causal claims. Examples: attributing national prosperity to a single institution merely because they coincided. Scoring: causal claims unsupported by elimination of alternatives should be rated weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false a priori theories that oversimplify causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorizing from assumed properties of a single agent while overlooking other co-existing agents (false theory) leads to erroneous conclusions; e.g., attributing all disease to one bodily property and treating that as sole causal explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize a priori causal theories for neglected factors and test them empirically. Beware schools of thought that reduce complex phenomena to a single hypothesized cause without elimination of alternatives or empirical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false analogies and do not overrate analogical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy only provides a weak increase in probability that what holds in one case holds in a similar case; it is not a substitute for induction from causally connected conditions and can be grossly misleading if its probative force is exaggerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat analogical reasoning as tentative and quantify its support: require demonstration of a causal connection between the shared property and the inferred property to upgrade the argument. Anti-patterns: drawing strong conclusions from superficial resemblances or from a single analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring resemblance in one respect implies resemblance in another (false analogy subtype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that because two cases are similar in property A they must be similar in property B—especially when evidence positively tends to disconnect A and B—is a fallacy (e.g., paternal government analogy to political despotism, metropolis size analogous to bodily disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the similarity pertains to the material circumstances relevant to the inferred property. If the key causal or conditional links are absent or contrary, the analogy fails. Examples from text: paternal authority ≠ political despotism; gold vs. corn analogy showing difference in how abundance affects utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious generalizing across times, societies, or cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing from phenomena observed in one age, country, or social condition to another (including projecting present conditions into the past or future) is frequently erroneous because causes combine differently across contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit empirical generalizations to 'adjacent cases' unless you can identify and justify the constancy of causal factors across contexts. Require analysis of the specific causes producing historical or social changes before extending generalizations beyond their observed scope.
